passages.title: Oppression and the midwives
passages.summary: Jacob’s seventy descendants in Egypt grow into a great people after Joseph dies. A new king who did not know Joseph fears their numbers. He sets taskmasters over them, and they build the store cities Pithom and Raamses. The harder Egypt presses them, the more they multiply. The king tells the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill newborn boys. The midwives fear God and let the boys live. God deals well with them and gives them families. Pharaoh then orders all his people to throw Hebrew baby boys into the river.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The midwives “feared God” and disobeyed the king (verse 17). What did Pharaoh fear in verses 9–10?

contextNote.title: Forced work and fear
contextNote.text: Pharaoh’s reason in verses 9–10 is fear, not any wrong Israel has done. He fears their numbers and what they might do in a war. Verse 11 turns that fear into policy: taskmasters and building work. The cities they build store goods for Pharaoh. Verse 12 shows the plan fail, since the people keep growing. So the king moves from hard labor to killing (verses 16 and 22). Genesis 47 showed how Egypt’s people became Pharaoh’s servants; now Israel is too.

passages.title: Moses preserved and exiled
passages.summary: A Levite woman bears a son and hides him three months. She puts him in a papyrus basket among the river reeds, and his sister watches. Pharaoh’s daughter finds him, pities him, and knows he is a Hebrew child. The sister offers a nurse and brings the boy’s own mother. Pharaoh’s daughter adopts him and names him Moses. Grown, Moses kills an Egyptian who beat a Hebrew, and he flees to Midian. He defends seven sisters at a well and marries one, Zipporah. Israel groans in slavery, and God hears and remembers his covenant.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Moses 1 expands Moses’s later encounter with God. Keep that account distinct from his childhood. Three women save the child in verses 2–10. Who are they?

contextNote.title: Women cross the boundaries that Pharaoh tries to enforce
contextNote.text: Pharaoh ordered every Hebrew boy thrown into the river (1:22). In verses 3–10 the river is where this boy is saved. His mother puts him there in a basket, and his sister guards him. Pharaoh’s own daughter knows he is Hebrew and keeps him anyway (verse 6). She even pays the mother to nurse her own son (verse 9). Verse 10 ends with a Hebrew child named and raised in the palace. None of the women is given an order by God in the text.

passages.title: The burning bush
passages.summary: Moses keeps his father-in-law’s flock and comes to Horeb, God’s mountain. He sees a bush on fire that does not burn up. God calls him by name and tells him to take off his sandals. The LORD has seen his people’s suffering and has come down to rescue them. He sends Moses to Pharaoh, and Moses asks, “Who am I?” God promises to be with him and gives his name: “I AM WHO I AM.” Moses must tell the elders and then ask Pharaoh for a three-day journey. God says Pharaoh will refuse until God strikes Egypt.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Exodus names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Church manual reads Moses’s call as preparation for prophetic service. The LORD says, “I know their sorrows” (verse 7). What does he say he has come down to do in verse 8?

contextNote.title: God's attention begins with the workers' suffering
contextNote.text: God’s first words about Israel are verbs of attention: seen, heard, know. Then verse 8 adds action: “I have come down to deliver them.” The cause named is “their taskmasters,” the men set over them in 1:11. So the rescue starts from the workers’ pain, not from Moses’s merit. Moses is sent in verse 10 as the means. His question in verse 11 is about himself. God’s answer in verse 12 is about God: “I will be with you.”

passages.title: Moses returns
passages.summary: Moses says the people will not believe him. The LORD gives him three signs with a rod, his hand, and river water. Moses says he is slow of speech and asks God to send someone else. The LORD is angry and names Aaron, his brother, to speak for him. Moses takes leave of Jethro and sets out with his wife and sons. The LORD tells him to call Israel “my firstborn” before Pharaoh. On the way the LORD meets him to kill him, and Zipporah circumcises her son. Aaron meets Moses, and the people believe and worship.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Moses asks the Lord to send someone else (verse 13). Whom does the LORD send with him in verses 14–16?

contextNote.title: A difficult calling makes room for shared speech
contextNote.text: Moses raises four objections across chapters 3 and 4. God answers each with a promise or a sign. The fifth, in verse 13, is not an objection but a refusal. Verse 14 says the LORD’s anger burned. Yet the answer is help, not removal: Aaron will be his mouth. God still says, “I will be with your mouth, and with his mouth” (verse 15). The task now needs two people who depend on each other.

passages.title: Pharaoh increases the burden
passages.summary: Moses and Aaron tell Pharaoh the LORD’s word: let my people go. Pharaoh says he does not know the LORD and will not let Israel go. He calls the people idle. That day he orders that they get no straw but make as many bricks. The people scatter to gather stubble, and their Israelite officers are beaten. The officers appeal to Pharaoh, and he repeats, “You are idle!” They blame Moses and Aaron. Moses asks the LORD why he sent him, since the people are not rescued.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Things get worse after Moses obeys. What does Moses say to the LORD in verses 22–23?

contextNote.title: The ruler makes the workers pay for the request
contextNote.text: Pharaoh answers a request to worship with a charge of laziness. Verse 17 repeats the charge: “You are idle!” He removes the straw and keeps the brick count (verse 18). The beating falls on Israel’s own officers, not on Moses (verse 14). So the officers turn on Moses and Aaron in verse 21. Pharaoh’s method sets the workers against the ones who spoke for them. Moses takes the complaint to the LORD in plain words (verses 22–23).

passages.title: God renews the promise
passages.summary: The LORD tells Moses that Pharaoh will drive Israel out by a strong hand. God says he is the LORD, who made a covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He has heard Israel groan and remembers that covenant. He promises to free them, take them as his people, and give them the land. The people do not listen, because of crushed spirits and cruel slavery. Moses asks how Pharaoh will listen if Israel will not. The chapter lists the families of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, down to Aaron and Moses. The LORD again sends Moses to Pharaoh.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The covenant promise includes belonging to God. The people cannot listen to Moses (verse 9). What two reasons does the verse give?

contextNote.title: Harsh labor changes what the people can hear
contextNote.text: Verses 6–8 hold seven promises that begin “I will.” They are the fullest promise in the book so far. Verse 9 reports that the people did not listen. The verse gives the cause, and it is not unbelief or rebellion. It is “anguish of spirit” and “cruel bondage.” The text does not blame them. God’s next word in verses 10–11 is to go on with the plan anyway.

passages.title: Staff and river
passages.summary: The LORD makes Moses like God to Pharaoh, with Aaron as his prophet. He says Pharaoh will not listen, and Egypt will learn that he is the LORD. Moses is eighty and Aaron eighty-three. Aaron’s rod becomes a serpent before Pharaoh, and it swallows the magicians’ rods. Pharaoh’s heart stays hard. In the morning Aaron strikes the river, and its water turns to blood. The fish die, and the Egyptians dig for water to drink. The magicians do the same, and Pharaoh goes home unmoved.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Pharaoh goes into his house and does not take it to heart (verse 23). What must ordinary Egyptians do in verse 24?

contextNote.title: The conflict reaches the water that sustains daily life
contextNote.text: The first plague strikes the river, the source of Egypt’s water and fish. Pharaoh had used that river to kill Hebrew boys (1:22). Verse 20 says the blow came “in the sight of Pharaoh.” Verse 23 shows him walk back into his house. Verse 24 shows his people digging along the bank for water. The king refuses, and those under him carry the cost. Verse 5 states the aim of it all: Egypt will know who the LORD is.

passages.title: Frogs, lice, and flies
passages.summary: Frogs come up from the river and fill houses, beds, and ovens. Pharaoh asks Moses to pray and promises to let the people go. The frogs die, and Pharaoh hardens his heart. Aaron strikes the dust, and it becomes lice on people and animals. The magicians cannot copy it and say, “This is God’s finger.” Swarms of flies fill Egypt, but not Goshen, where Israel lives. Pharaoh offers a sacrifice inside Egypt, then a short trip into the wilderness. Moses prays, the flies leave, and Pharaoh again refuses.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Pharaoh says Israel may go, “only you shall not go very far away” (verse 28). What happens to his promise in verse 32?

contextNote.title: Permission offered under pressure remains restricted
contextNote.text: Pharaoh bargains twice in this chapter. In verse 25 he allows worship but only “in the land.” In verse 28 he allows the wilderness but not “very far away.” Each offer gives a little and keeps control. He also asks, “Pray for me,” while the flies are still there. Moses warns him in verse 29 not to deal falsely again. Verses 15 and 32 show the pattern: relief comes, and the promise ends.

passages.title: Livestock, boils, and hail
passages.summary: A disease kills Egypt’s livestock in the field, but none of Israel’s animals die. Moses throws furnace ashes into the air, and boils break out on people and animals. The magicians cannot stand before Moses. The LORD says he let Pharaoh stand to show his power in all the earth. He warns of heavy hail and tells Egypt to bring servants and animals inside. Some of Pharaoh’s servants fear the word and obey; others do not. Hail and fire strike all Egypt except Goshen. Pharaoh says he has sinned, but when the hail stops he hardens his heart.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Pharaoh says, “I have sinned this time” (verse 27). What does verse 34 say he did when the hail stopped?

contextNote.title: People within Egypt do not respond in one way
contextNote.text: The hail is the first plague that comes with a way to escape. Verse 19 tells Egypt to bring people and animals under cover. Verses 20–21 then divide Pharaoh’s own servants into two groups. Some “feared the LORD’s word” and saved their workers and herds. Others left them in the field. So Egyptians are not treated as one mass, and some respond before their king does. In 10:7 those servants urge Pharaoh to give in.

passages.title: Locusts and darkness
passages.summary: The LORD says these signs are for Israel to tell their children and grandchildren. Moses warns of locusts, and Pharaoh’s servants beg him to let the men go. Pharaoh asks who will go, and Moses says everyone, with flocks and herds. Pharaoh will let only the men go and drives Moses out. Locusts eat every green thing the hail left. Pharaoh admits sin, the locusts are blown into the Red Sea, and he refuses again. Three days of thick darkness cover Egypt, but Israel has light. Pharaoh says to go but leave the animals, and Moses says not a hoof stays.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Pharaoh will let the people go if the flocks stay (verse 24). Why does Moses say every animal must come in verse 26?

contextNote.title: Control continues through what the people must leave behind
contextNote.text: Pharaoh has now offered four deals. Worship in Egypt, not too far, men only, and now people without animals. Each one keeps something of Israel’s in his hand. Flocks left behind would be a reason to return. Moses gives a different reason in verse 26: the animals are for the LORD. They do not yet know what he will ask for. So Moses will not agree to limits on worship before it begins.

passages.title: The final plague announced
passages.summary: The LORD tells Moses that one more plague will make Pharaoh drive Israel out. The people are to ask their Egyptian neighbors for silver and gold. Moses is highly regarded in Egypt. He tells Pharaoh the LORD will go through Egypt about midnight. Every firstborn will die, from Pharaoh’s son to the slave girl’s at the mill. A great cry will rise, but not a dog will bark at Israel. Moses leaves Pharaoh in hot anger. The LORD hardens Pharaoh’s heart, and he still refuses.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The plague reaches from the throne to the slave at the mill (verse 5). How do these deaths affect your reading of Israel’s freedom?

contextNote.title: Royal refusal creates danger beyond the royal household
contextNote.text: Verse 5 names the top and the bottom of Egypt. Pharaoh sits on a throne, and the servant woman sits behind a millstone. Both lose a firstborn, and so does the livestock. The servant had no part in Pharaoh’s decisions. In 4:22–23 God called Israel his firstborn and warned of this exact result. Pharaoh’s refusals in chapters 5–10 bring the loss on his whole land. The text reports the cry in verse 6 without softening it.

passages.title: Passover and departure
passages.summary: The LORD makes this month the first of the year. Each household must take a lamb without defect and kill it on the fourteenth day. They put its blood on the door posts and eat it roasted, dressed to leave. The LORD will strike Egypt’s firstborn and pass over the houses with blood. Israel must keep this day and seven days of bread without yeast, forever. At midnight every Egyptian house has someone dead, and Pharaoh tells Israel to go. They leave in haste with unrisen dough and Egyptian silver and gold. About 600,000 men leave on foot, with a mixed crowd, after 430 years.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the Passover lamb with Jesus Christ. Children will ask what the Passover service means (verse 26). What answer does verse 27 give?

contextNote.title: A meal makes departure available to later generations
contextNote.text: The rules for the meal are given before the rescue happens. Verses 14, 17, and 24 each say to keep it in later generations. Verse 26 expects a child’s question at the table. The answer in verse 27 says the LORD “spared our houses.” A parent born long after can still say “our.” So the meal lets each generation stand inside the night of leaving. Verse 11 keeps the hurry in it: belt on, sandals on, staff in hand.

passages.title: Remembering and the pillars
passages.summary: The LORD claims every firstborn male in Israel, human and animal. Moses tells the people to remember this day with seven days of unleavened bread. They must tell their sons what the LORD did when they left Egypt. Firstborn animals are sacrificed, and firstborn sons are bought back. God does not lead them by the near road through Philistine land. He says they might see war and return to Egypt. He leads them by the wilderness toward the Red Sea, and Moses carries Joseph’s bones. The LORD goes ahead in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: God chose the longer road (verses 17–18). What reason does verse 17 give?

contextNote.title: The journey accounts for fear as well as distance
contextNote.text: Verse 17 says the short road was near and God did not use it. The reason is the people, not the distance. They might see war, change their minds, and go back to Egypt. So the route is fitted to what they can bear. Verse 18 notes they left “armed,” yet arms did not make them ready. Verses 21–22 add that they are not left to find the way alone. The cloud and fire never leave the front of the camp.

passages.title: The sea crossing
passages.summary: The LORD has Israel camp by the sea, so Pharaoh will think they are trapped. Pharaoh regrets freeing his slaves and chases them with six hundred chosen chariots. The people see the army, cry out, and tell Moses that serving Egypt was better. Moses says to stand still and see the LORD’s rescue. The cloud moves behind Israel, between the two camps. Moses stretches out his hand, and an east wind divides the sea all night. Israel crosses on dry ground with walls of water on each side. The Egyptians follow, the water returns, and not one of them is left.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Exodus names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: First Nephi 17 recalls the sea crossing to teach trust in God. The people say serving Egypt was better (verse 12). What does Moses tell them to do in verses 13–14?

contextNote.title: Fear makes the old dependence appear safer
contextNote.text: The people have only just left Egypt. In verse 12 they quote what they said there: “Leave us alone.” Slavery was hard, but it was known, and the sea and the army are not. So fear makes the old life look safe. Moses does not argue with them. He tells them to stand still and watch (verses 13–14). Verse 31 shows the change afterward: they fear the LORD and believe.

passages.title: Songs and bitter water
passages.summary: Moses and Israel sing to the LORD, who threw horse and rider into the sea. The song says the LORD is a warrior, and Pharaoh’s captains sank like a stone. It says the nations tremble and the LORD will plant his people on his mountain. Miriam the prophetess leads the women with tambourines and dancing. Israel then walks three days in the wilderness without water. At Marah the water is bitter, and the people grumble at Moses. The LORD shows Moses a tree that makes the water sweet. He promises health if they listen, and they camp at Elim’s twelve springs.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Exodus names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Three days after the song, the people ask Moses what they will drink (verse 24). What does the LORD call himself in verse 26?

contextNote.title: The song ends before the need for water ends
contextNote.text: Verses 1–21 are a long song of praise. Verse 22 follows with three days and no water. The singers of verse 1 are the grumblers of verse 24. The text does not hide how fast that happened. Their need is real, and the LORD answers it without rebuke in verse 25. He also calls this a test and adds a promise tied to listening (verse 26). Verse 27 ends with more water than they asked for: twelve springs.

passages.title: Manna and Sabbath
passages.summary: In the second month Israel reaches the wilderness of Sin and complains of hunger. They say they wish they had died by the meat pots of Egypt. The LORD promises bread from the sky each day, as a test. Quail come at evening, and a fine flake covers the ground at dawn. Each person gathers an omer, and no one has too much or too little. What is kept overnight rots, except on the sixth day, when they gather double. On the seventh day there is none, because it is the Sabbath. They call it manna and eat it forty years.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Exodus names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Church manual connects manna with reliance on God. Some gathered more and some less (verse 17). What does verse 18 say each one ended with?

contextNote.title: Food becomes a test of community
contextNote.text: The bread comes with rules, and verse 4 calls them a test. Each household takes one omer per person (verse 16). Verse 18 gives the result: no one had extra, and no one lacked. Hoarding fails, since kept manna rots by morning (verse 20). So no one can store up an advantage over a neighbor. In Egypt they were measured by bricks made. Here they are measured by what each one needs to eat.

passages.title: Water and Amalek
passages.summary: Israel camps at Rephidim, where there is no water. The people quarrel with Moses and say he brought them out to die. Moses cries to the LORD and says they are ready to stone him. He strikes the rock at Horeb before the elders, and water comes out. The place is named Massah and Meribah for their testing and quarrel. Amalek attacks, and Joshua leads the fight while Moses stands on the hill. Israel wins while Moses’ hands are up, so Aaron and Hur hold them until sunset. Moses builds an altar named “The LORD our Banner.”
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Exodus names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Moses cannot keep his hands up alone (verse 12). Who helps him, and how?

contextNote.title: The battle depends on support that the account makes visible
contextNote.text: Verse 11 ties the battle to Moses’ raised hand. Verse 12 then admits a plain limit: his hands grew heavy. The fix is ordinary. Two men bring a stone for him to sit on and hold his arms. Joshua fights below, Moses holds the rod, and Aaron and Hur hold Moses. The account names every one of them. In verse 15 the altar’s name gives the credit to the LORD.

passages.title: Jethro's counsel
passages.summary: Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law and priest of Midian, hears what the LORD did for Israel. He brings Moses’ wife Zipporah and their two sons to the camp. Moses tells him everything, and Jethro blesses the LORD and offers sacrifices. The next day Moses judges the people alone from morning to evening. Jethro says this is not good and will wear out Moses and the people. He advises choosing honest, able men to judge small cases. Hard cases will still come to Moses. Moses does all this, and Jethro goes home.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Jethro tells Moses, “The thing that you do is not good” (verse 17). Who gains from his plan in verse 23?

contextNote.title: Accessible judgment requires more than one capable leader
contextNote.text: Jethro watches a full day of court before he speaks (verses 13–14). His worry in verse 18 is for two parties: Moses and the people. One judge means people stand waiting from morning to evening. Verse 21 sets the test for new judges: able, God-fearing, truthful, and hating unjust gain. Verse 23 names both gains. Moses will last, and the people “will go to their place in peace.” The advice comes from a Midianite priest, and Moses takes it (verse 24).

passages.title: At Sinai
passages.summary: In the third month Israel camps before Mount Sinai. The LORD reminds them how he carried them on eagles’ wings. If they keep his covenant, they will be his own, a kingdom of priests. All the people answer that they will do what the LORD has spoken. They wash their clothes, and a boundary is set around the mountain. On the third day there is thunder, lightning, thick cloud, and a loud trumpet. The mountain smokes and shakes as the LORD comes down in fire. Moses goes up and is sent back to warn the people.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Exodus names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Church manual connects covenant belonging with duties of holiness and service. The people answer together in verse 8. What had God done for them before he asked (verse 4)?

contextNote.title: A rescued people must answer an offered relationship
contextNote.text: God’s offer in verses 4–6 starts with what he has already done. He brought them out and “brought you to myself.” Only then comes the “if” of verse 5. So the covenant is offered to a freed people, not to slaves earning freedom. Verse 8 records their answer before any law is given. They agree to the relationship first and hear its terms in chapter 20. Verse 6 states their role toward others: a kingdom of priests.

passages.title: The Ten Commandments
passages.summary: God speaks and names himself as the one who brought Israel out of slavery. He commands no other gods, no idols, and no misuse of his name. The seventh day is a Sabbath of rest for children, servants, animals, and strangers. They must honor father and mother. They must not murder, commit adultery, steal, give false testimony, or covet. The people tremble at the thunder and smoke and stand far off. They ask Moses to speak for God, and Moses goes into the thick darkness. The LORD forbids gods of silver or gold and allows a plain altar of earth.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual studies how each command can shape faithful choices. The Sabbath command names who must rest (verse 10). Who is on the list besides the head of the house?

contextNote.title: Rest limits the household's power over others
contextNote.text: Verse 2 comes before any command: God freed them from “the house of bondage.” The Sabbath command takes four verses (8–11). Verse 10 lists who may not be made to work: children, servants, animals, and strangers. The one addressed is the person with power to order others. So the day of rest limits what a master may demand. Egypt allowed no rest from bricks (5:5–9). Verse 11 roots the day in God’s own rest at creation.

passages.title: Laws about servants and injury
passages.summary: These are the rulings set before Israel. A Hebrew servant serves six years and goes free in the seventh. A daughter sold as a servant keeps rights to food and clothing, or goes free. Murder brings death, but an accidental killer may flee to a set place. Kidnapping and striking or cursing parents bring death. One who injures another pays for lost time and healing. A master who destroys a servant’s eye or tooth must free that servant. Owners pay for harm from an open pit or a bull known to gore.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: These laws come from an ancient legal setting. A servant who loses an eye goes free (verse 26). What does verse 21 show about the servant’s standing?

contextNote.title: Injury rules reveal both protection and unequal status
contextNote.text: These rulings assume that some people are servants owned by others. Verse 21 calls the servant the master’s “property.” Within that world, verses 26–27 set a limit. A master who destroys an eye or knocks out a tooth loses the servant. The injured person goes free “for his eye’s sake.” So the servant’s body is protected, though the servant is not equal. Verse 2 adds a time limit: a Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year.

passages.title: Property and vulnerable people
passages.summary: A thief pays back more than he stole, up to five oxen for one. A person pays for crops ruined by his animal or his fire. Disputes over goods left in another’s care come before God. A man who seduces an unpledged virgin must pay a dowry for her. Israel must not wrong a foreigner, because they were foreigners in Egypt. God will hear the cry of any widow or fatherless child they wrong. Lenders must not charge the poor interest. A cloak taken as a pledge must be returned before sunset.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: A poor borrower’s cloak must be returned by sunset (verse 26). What reason does verse 27 give?

contextNote.title: A loan cannot remove the borrower's means to endure the night
contextNote.text: A lender could hold a cloak as security for a loan. Verse 26 lets the pledge be taken but not kept overnight. Verse 27 explains with a question: “What would he sleep in?” The cloak is the poor man’s only cover. So the law puts his night’s sleep above the lender’s security. God says he will hear the borrower’s cry, “for I am gracious.” Verse 23 makes the same promise to widows and the fatherless.

passages.title: Justice, rest, and festivals
passages.summary: Israel must not spread false reports or follow a crowd to do evil. Judges must not favor the poor or deny them justice, and must refuse bribes. A person must return an enemy’s stray ox and help his fallen donkey. Israel must not oppress foreigners, since they know a foreigner’s heart. The land rests every seventh year so the poor may eat. The seventh day gives rest to animals, servants, and foreigners. Three feasts are kept each year. God will send an angel ahead and drive out the nations little by little.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The law tells Israel to help the donkey of “him who hates you” (verse 5). What does the helper have to set aside?

contextNote.title: An enemy's need can interrupt personal hostility
contextNote.text: Verses 1–9 are mostly about fair courts. Verses 4–5 sit in the middle and deal with an enemy. His ox has strayed, or his donkey has fallen under its load. The law does not ask what the owner deserves. It says, “You shall surely help him.” The animal’s need and the owner’s loss come before the grudge. The court rules around it ask for the same fairness toward everyone.

passages.title: The covenant confirmed
passages.summary: The LORD calls Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders to come up and worship. Moses tells the people all the LORD’s words, and they promise to do them. He writes the words down and builds an altar with twelve pillars. He reads the book of the covenant aloud, and the people again promise to obey. Moses sprinkles blood on the altar and on the people. The leaders go up, see the God of Israel, and eat and drink. The LORD calls Moses higher to receive stone tablets. Moses enters the cloud and stays forty days and nights.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: A covenant includes an informed promise. The people promise after hearing the book read (verse 7). What did they promise before, in verse 3?

contextNote.title: The agreement follows a public reading of its terms
contextNote.text: The people agree three times: in 19:8, in verse 3, and in verse 7. Between the second and third, Moses writes the words down (verse 4). Then he reads the book “in the hearing of the people.” Only after that reading is the blood sprinkled on them (verse 8). So they bind themselves to terms they have heard in full. An Egyptian scribe’s palette shows writing tools from that world. Verse 12 adds stone tablets written by God.

passages.title: The ark, table, and lampstand
passages.summary: The LORD tells Moses to take an offering from everyone with a willing heart. The gifts are gold, silver, bronze, fine cloth, skins, wood, oil, spices, and stones. The people are to make a sanctuary so that God may live among them. They must follow the pattern God shows Moses. The ark is a gold-covered chest with poles, and it holds the covenant. Its gold cover, the mercy seat, has two cherubim, and God will meet Moses there. A gold-covered table holds the bread of the presence. A lamp stand of pure gold has seven lamps.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the tabernacle with worship and God’s presence among His people. God gives the reason for the sanctuary in verse 8. What is it?

contextNote.title: The sanctuary brings presence into a traveling community
contextNote.text: Verse 8 gives the purpose of everything in chapters 25–31. God wants to “dwell among them,” in the camp. Until now he has met Israel on a mountain they could not touch (19:12). The ark and the table get poles for carrying (verses 14 and 28). So God’s dwelling moves when the people move. The materials come only from those “whose heart makes him willing” (verse 2). The house is asked for, not taken by force.

passages.title: The tabernacle structure
passages.summary: The tabernacle is made of ten linen curtains in blue, purple, and scarlet, with cherubim. Gold clasps join them into one piece. A cover of goats’ hair goes over it, then ram skins and hides. Upright boards of acacia wood stand in silver sockets and are held by bars. All of it follows what Moses saw on the mountain. A veil with cherubim hangs on four pillars inside. The ark goes behind the veil, in the most holy place. The table and lamp stand stay outside the veil, and a screen covers the door.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The veil separates the holy place from the most holy (verse 33). What is placed behind it?

contextNote.title: A veil gives the tent an ordered interior
contextNote.text: Most of the chapter is measurements, loops, clasps, and boards. Verse 33 says what the layout is for. A veil divides the tent into two rooms: the holy place and the most holy. The ark, with the covenant inside, goes in the inner room (verses 33–34). The table and lamp go in the outer room (verse 35). So the nearer a space is to the ark, the more it is set apart. God lives in the camp (25:8), yet the tent keeps a boundary around him.

passages.title: Altar, court, and light
passages.summary: The altar is square, made of acacia wood covered with bronze, with horns. Its pots, shovels, basins, and grating are bronze, and poles carry it. The court around the tabernacle is one hundred cubits long and fifty wide. Linen hangings on bronze-footed pillars form its walls. A screen of blue, purple, and scarlet covers the gate. The people of Israel must bring pure beaten olive oil for the lamp. Aaron and his sons keep the lamp burning from evening to morning. This is a lasting rule for Israel.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The lamp must burn “continually” (verse 20). Who supplies the oil, and who tends the lamp?

contextNote.title: Continuing light requires continuing contributions
contextNote.text: Verses 1–19 describe things that are built once. Verses 20–21 describe something that must be done every day. The lamp burns only if oil keeps coming. The oil comes from “the children of Israel,” not from the priests’ own stores. Aaron and his sons tend it each night for the people of Israel. So the light depends on both groups doing a repeated task. A finished building does not keep itself lit.

passages.title: The priests' clothing
passages.summary: Aaron and his four sons become priests, and skilled workers make Aaron’s holy garments. The ephod, a priestly garment, has two shoulder stones with the names of Israel’s sons. The breastplate holds twelve stones, one for each tribe. Aaron carries the names over his heart when he enters the holy place. The Urim and Thummim go in the breastplate. A blue robe has gold bells on its hem. A gold plate on his forehead says “HOLY TO THE LORD.” His sons receive tunics, sashes, and headbands.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Aaron carries Israel’s names on his shoulders and over his heart (verses 12 and 29). For whom does he go into the holy place?

contextNote.title: The priest carries names rather than only personal status
contextNote.text: The garments are costly, and verse 2 says they are “for glory and for beauty.” Yet the two main pieces carry other people’s names. The shoulder stones hold the names of Israel’s sons (verse 12). The breastplate holds twelve stones for the twelve tribes (verse 21). Verse 29 says Aaron bears them “on his heart” whenever he goes in. He does not enter the holy place as a private person. He stands there for the whole people, tribe by tribe.

passages.title: Consecrating the priests
passages.summary: Moses is told how to make Aaron and his sons priests. They are washed, dressed in the holy garments, and anointed with oil. A bull is offered for sin, and a ram is burned whole. Blood from a second ram goes on each priest’s right ear, thumb, and big toe. The priests eat their share of that ram at the tent door. The rites last seven days and also make the altar holy. After that two lambs are offered every day, one at morning and one at evening. God says he will meet Israel there and live among them.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual studies preparation for sacred service. After seven days of rites, God states his aim in verses 45–46. What is it?

contextNote.title: Priestly preparation serves a larger purpose of presence
contextNote.text: The chapter spends forty-four verses on washing, clothing, blood, and food. Verse 45 gives the purpose: “I will dwell among the children of Israel.” Verse 46 links that to the exodus itself. God brought them out of Egypt “that I might dwell among them.” So the priests are a means, not the goal. The same is true of the altar and the daily lambs (verses 38–43). Freedom from Pharaoh was meant to end in living with God.

passages.title: Incense, washing, and sacred oil
passages.summary: A small gold altar for incense stands before the veil. Aaron burns incense on it every morning and evening. When Israel is counted, each man twenty and older gives half a shekel. The rich give no more and the poor no less. The money serves the Tent of Meeting. A bronze basin holds water for the priests to wash hands and feet. A holy spiced oil anoints the tent, its furniture, and the priests. No one may copy the oil or the incense for private use.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Rich and poor pay the same half shekel (verse 15). What does the verse say the payment is for?

contextNote.title: A required payment does not measure people by their wealth
contextNote.text: Most gifts for the tent were free and varied by what people had (25:2). This payment is different. Verse 12 calls it “a ransom for his soul,” given when the people are counted. Verse 15 fixes it at half a shekel for everyone. A rich man cannot pay for more, and a poor man counts no less. Each life is set at the same value before the LORD. Verse 16 says the money goes to the tent, as a reminder for all Israel.

passages.title: Skilled workers and Sabbath
passages.summary: The LORD names Bezalel of Judah and fills him with God’s Spirit and skill. He will work in gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood. Oholiab of Dan will work with him, and other skilled people will help. They are to make the tent, its furniture, the garments, the oil, and the incense. Then the LORD says Israel must surely keep his Sabbaths. The Sabbath is a sign between God and Israel for all generations. Six days are for work, and the seventh is holy rest. God gives Moses two stone tablets written with his finger.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Right after naming the builders, God commands the Sabbath (verse 13). Why might the two be placed together?

contextNote.title: Sacred construction does not cancel the command to rest
contextNote.text: Verses 1–11 assign the work of building God’s tent. Verse 13 follows at once with the Sabbath. The wording is strong: “Most certainly you shall keep my Sabbaths.” Even work on God’s own tent stops on the seventh day. Verse 13 calls the day a sign that the LORD makes Israel holy. So their holiness comes from him, not from how much they build. Verse 17 adds that God himself rested and was refreshed.

passages.title: The golden calf
passages.summary: Moses delays on the mountain, and the people ask Aaron to make gods. Aaron collects their gold earrings and makes a calf. The people say these gods brought them out of Egypt, and they feast. The LORD tells Moses he will destroy them, and Moses pleads for them. The LORD turns from the harm he spoke of. Moses comes down, sees the calf and dancing, and breaks the tablets. He grinds the calf to powder, and Aaron blames the people and the fire. The Levites kill about three thousand, and Moses asks God to forgive the people.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The people call the calf the gods who brought them out of Egypt (verse 4). Whom had they just promised to obey in 24:7?

contextNote.title: Freedom does not remove the desire for visible gods
contextNote.text: The people do not ask to go back to Egypt. They ask for gods to “go before us” because Moses is gone (verse 1). The gold is their own earrings, shaped by Aaron with a tool (verses 3–4). Then they give the calf the credit for the exodus. Aaron calls the next day “a feast to the LORD” (verse 5). Aaron ties the calf to the LORD’s name, though 20:4 forbade images. In verse 24 Aaron says the calf just came out of the fire.

passages.title: Moses seeks God's presence
passages.summary: The LORD tells Moses to lead the people on, with an angel ahead. He says he will not go among them, because they are stubborn. The people mourn and take off their jewelry. Moses pitches a tent outside the camp, and the cloud comes down when he enters. The LORD speaks with Moses face to face, as with a friend. Moses says that if God’s presence does not go, they should not leave. The LORD agrees to go with them. Moses asks to see God’s glory and is allowed to see his back.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: God offers the land with an angel but without himself (verses 2–3). What does Moses say in verse 15?

contextNote.title: Arrival alone would not complete the purpose of rescue
contextNote.text: Verses 1–3 offer Israel everything except God’s company. They would get the land, an angel, and victory. The people mourn at this in verse 4, and Moses refuses it in verse 15. He says not to move them at all without God’s presence. Verse 16 gives his reason: God going with them is what sets them apart. This matches 29:46, where God freed them in order to dwell among them. The land alone was never the goal.

passages.title: The covenant renewed
passages.summary: Moses cuts two new stone tablets and goes up Sinai alone. The LORD comes down in the cloud and declares his name. He is merciful, slow to anger, and forgiving, yet does not clear the guilty. Moses bows and asks God to go with this stubborn people and pardon them. The LORD makes a covenant and promises wonders. Israel must make no treaty with the people of the land or worship their gods. The feasts, firstborn, and Sabbath laws are repeated. Moses comes down with a shining face and afterward wears a veil.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual reads renewal alongside repentance. The LORD describes himself after the calf (verses 6–7). Which words come first?

contextNote.title: Renewal holds mercy beside continuing consequences
contextNote.text: Israel has just broken the covenant with the calf (chapter 32). God’s first words about himself now are “merciful and gracious.” More follow before any warning: slow to anger, loving kindness, truth, forgiving. Then verse 7 adds that he “will by no means clear the guilty.” Both halves stand, and neither cancels the other. Mercy reaches thousands, and the harm of sin reaches three or four generations. Moses answers by asking for pardon and God’s presence (verse 9).

passages.title: Gifts and willing work
passages.summary: Moses gathers all Israel and repeats the Sabbath rule first. Then he asks for an offering from everyone with a willing heart. He lists what must be made, from the tent to the priests’ garments. Men and women bring gold jewelry, cloth, skins, silver, bronze, and wood. Skilled women spin the colored yarn and the goats’ hair. The rulers bring stones, spice, and oil. All of it is a free offering to the LORD. Moses names Bezalel and Oholiab, whom God filled with skill to work and teach.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Men and women bring gifts because their hearts are willing (verse 29). How does this work differ from the brick making in chapter 5?

contextNote.title: Willing labor contrasts with the labor that began the book
contextNote.text: Exodus began with forced building for Pharaoh (1:11–14). It ends with building for God, and the word used again and again is “willing.” Verses 5, 21, 22, 26, and 29 all tie the gifts to the heart. No taskmaster sets a quota. Women are named as givers and as skilled spinners (verses 22 and 25–26). The gold comes after the calf, when gold was given for an idol (32:3). Verse 2 puts Sabbath rest ahead of the work itself.

passages.title: More than enough
passages.summary: Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled worker begin the work. The people keep bringing free gifts every morning. The workers tell Moses there is far more than enough. Moses orders that no one bring anything more, and the people stop. The workers make the ten linen curtains with cherubim and join them with gold clasps. They make the goats’ hair covering and the skin coverings. They set up acacia boards in silver sockets and overlay them with gold. They make the veil and the screen for the door.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The people give so much that Moses tells them to stop (verse 6). What does that say about the purpose of the collection?

contextNote.title: A finished purpose sets a limit on collecting gifts
contextNote.text: The workers, not Moses, report the surplus in verse 5. Their honest report ends the collection. Moses then sends word through the camp to stop giving (verse 6). Verse 7 states the reason: there was enough for the work, and more. The gifts were for a set task, so the task sets the limit. Pharaoh raised the demand when workers asked for rest (5:8). Here the leader lowers it when the need is met.

passages.title: The furnishings made
passages.summary: Bezalel makes the ark of acacia wood and covers it with gold inside and out. He makes its rings and poles for carrying. He makes the gold mercy seat with two cherubim facing each other. He makes the gold-covered table and its dishes. He makes the lamp stand from one piece of pure gold, with seven lamps. He makes the gold incense altar with its poles. He makes the holy oil and the incense.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Bezalel makes the ark as 25:10–11 described (verses 1–2). Why might the book repeat each detail?

contextNote.title: Repeated details connect a plan with its fulfillment
contextNote.text: This chapter repeats chapter 25 almost line for line. There the verbs said “you shall make.” Here they say “he made.” The sizes in verse 1 match 25:10 exactly. Between the plan and the work came the calf and the broken tablets. The careful repeat shows that the plan was still carried out in full. The work is credited to a named craftsman, Bezalel, not to Moses.

passages.title: Altar, court, and accounts
passages.summary: Bezalel makes the bronze altar for burnt offerings with its tools and poles. He makes the bronze basin from the mirrors of women serving at the tent. He makes the court with linen hangings, bronze sockets, and silver hooks. Then the chapter gives the amounts of the materials. Ithamar, Aaron’s son, kept the count for the Levites. The gold weighed over twenty-nine talents. The silver came from the half shekel paid by 603,550 men. The bronze weighed over seventy talents, and each metal’s use is listed.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The chapter lists how much gold, silver, and bronze was used (verses 24–31). Who kept the count, according to verse 21?

contextNote.title: Sacred work includes an account of its materials
contextNote.text: The people gave freely in chapter 35. Verse 21 shows that their gifts were then counted. Moses ordered the count, and Ithamar the priest kept it. Verses 24–29 give totals for gold, silver, and bronze. Verses 27–31 say what each metal was made into. So the givers could know where their gifts went. Verse 8 keeps one gift in view by name: the women’s mirrors became the basin.

passages.title: Garments and inspection
passages.summary: The workers make Aaron’s holy garments from blue, purple, and scarlet yarn. They beat gold into thin wires and weave it into the ephod. They set the onyx shoulder stones and the twelve stones of the breastplate. They make the blue robe with bells and pomegranates on its hem. They make tunics, turbans, and sashes, and the gold plate reading “HOLY TO THE LORD.” All the work is finished as the LORD commanded Moses. The people bring every part to Moses. He inspects it and blesses them.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Moses looks over all the work before he blesses the people (verse 43). What did he find?

contextNote.title: A blessing follows examination of completed work
contextNote.text: The phrase “as the LORD commanded Moses” ends seven steps in verses 1–31. Verse 32 says the same of the whole people. Then they bring the parts to Moses, and verses 33–41 list each one. Moses looks at everything before he speaks. Verse 43 says he “saw all the work” and found it done as commanded. Only then does he bless them. Genesis 1:31 and 2:3 show the same order: God sees, then blesses.

passages.title: The tabernacle raised
passages.summary: The LORD tells Moses to raise the tabernacle on the year’s first day. Moses puts the covenant in the ark and hangs the veil in front of it. He sets the table, the lamp stand, and the incense altar in their places. He puts the altar of burnt offering and the basin outside. He anoints the tent and washes and dresses Aaron and his sons. Moses finishes the work, and the cloud covers the tent. The LORD’s glory fills it, and Moses cannot enter. Israel travels when the cloud lifts and stays when it rests.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the sanctuary with God’s presence. The cloud fills the tent and also leads the journey (verses 34–38). What do the people do when it lifts?

contextNote.title: The completed dwelling still belongs to a moving people
contextNote.text: Verse 34 is the goal the book has moved toward since 25:8. God’s glory fills the tent in the middle of the camp. Even Moses cannot go in (verse 35). Yet the book does not end with the people settled. Verses 36–37 make the cloud the signal to pack up or stay. The tent was built with poles and rings for this reason. God lives with a people who are still on the road.

events.title: Oppression and the midwives
events.summary: Jacob’s seventy descendants in Egypt grow into a great people after Joseph dies. A new king who did not know Joseph fears their numbers. He sets taskmasters over them, and they build the store cities Pithom and Raamses. The harder Egypt presses them, the more they multiply. The king tells the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill newborn boys. The midwives fear God and let the boys live. God deals well with them and gives them families. Pharaoh then orders all his people to throw Hebrew baby boys into the river.
events.detail: Pharaoh’s reason in verses 9–10 is fear, not any wrong Israel has done. He fears their numbers and what they might do in a war. Verse 11 turns that fear into policy: taskmasters and building work. The cities they build store goods for Pharaoh. Verse 12 shows the plan fail, since the people keep growing. So the king moves from hard labor to killing (verses 16 and 22). Genesis 47 showed how Egypt’s people became Pharaoh’s servants; now Israel is too.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The midwives “feared God” and disobeyed the king (verse 17). What did Pharaoh fear in verses 9–10?

events.title: Moses preserved and exiled
events.summary: A Levite woman bears a son and hides him three months. She puts him in a papyrus basket among the river reeds, and his sister watches. Pharaoh’s daughter finds him, pities him, and knows he is a Hebrew child. The sister offers a nurse and brings the boy’s own mother. Pharaoh’s daughter adopts him and names him Moses. Grown, Moses kills an Egyptian who beat a Hebrew, and he flees to Midian. He defends seven sisters at a well and marries one, Zipporah. Israel groans in slavery, and God hears and remembers his covenant.
events.detail: Pharaoh ordered every Hebrew boy thrown into the river (1:22). In verses 3–10 the river is where this boy is saved. His mother puts him there in a basket, and his sister guards him. Pharaoh’s own daughter knows he is Hebrew and keeps him anyway (verse 6). She even pays the mother to nurse her own son (verse 9). Verse 10 ends with a Hebrew child named and raised in the palace. None of the women is given an order by God in the text.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Moses 1 expands Moses’s later encounter with God. Keep that account distinct from his childhood. Three women save the child in verses 2–10. Who are they?

events.title: The burning bush
events.summary: Moses keeps his father-in-law’s flock and comes to Horeb, God’s mountain. He sees a bush on fire that does not burn up. God calls him by name and tells him to take off his sandals. The LORD has seen his people’s suffering and has come down to rescue them. He sends Moses to Pharaoh, and Moses asks, “Who am I?” God promises to be with him and gives his name: “I AM WHO I AM.” Moses must tell the elders and then ask Pharaoh for a three-day journey. God says Pharaoh will refuse until God strikes Egypt.
events.detail: God’s first words about Israel are verbs of attention: seen, heard, know. Then verse 8 adds action: “I have come down to deliver them.” The cause named is “their taskmasters,” the men set over them in 1:11. So the rescue starts from the workers’ pain, not from Moses’s merit. Moses is sent in verse 10 as the means. His question in verse 11 is about himself. God’s answer in verse 12 is about God: “I will be with you.”
events.uncertainty: Lines join the places Exodus names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Church manual reads Moses’s call as preparation for prophetic service. The LORD says, “I know their sorrows” (verse 7). What does he say he has come down to do in verse 8?

events.title: Moses returns
events.summary: Moses says the people will not believe him. The LORD gives him three signs with a rod, his hand, and river water. Moses says he is slow of speech and asks God to send someone else. The LORD is angry and names Aaron, his brother, to speak for him. Moses takes leave of Jethro and sets out with his wife and sons. The LORD tells him to call Israel “my firstborn” before Pharaoh. On the way the LORD meets him to kill him, and Zipporah circumcises her son. Aaron meets Moses, and the people believe and worship.
events.detail: Moses raises four objections across chapters 3 and 4. God answers each with a promise or a sign. The fifth, in verse 13, is not an objection but a refusal. Verse 14 says the LORD’s anger burned. Yet the answer is help, not removal: Aaron will be his mouth. God still says, “I will be with your mouth, and with his mouth” (verse 15). The task now needs two people who depend on each other.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Moses asks the Lord to send someone else (verse 13). Whom does the LORD send with him in verses 14–16?

events.title: Pharaoh increases the burden
events.summary: Moses and Aaron tell Pharaoh the LORD’s word: let my people go. Pharaoh says he does not know the LORD and will not let Israel go. He calls the people idle. That day he orders that they get no straw but make as many bricks. The people scatter to gather stubble, and their Israelite officers are beaten. The officers appeal to Pharaoh, and he repeats, “You are idle!” They blame Moses and Aaron. Moses asks the LORD why he sent him, since the people are not rescued.
events.detail: Pharaoh answers a request to worship with a charge of laziness. Verse 17 repeats the charge: “You are idle!” He removes the straw and keeps the brick count (verse 18). The beating falls on Israel’s own officers, not on Moses (verse 14). So the officers turn on Moses and Aaron in verse 21. Pharaoh’s method sets the workers against the ones who spoke for them. Moses takes the complaint to the LORD in plain words (verses 22–23).
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Things get worse after Moses obeys. What does Moses say to the LORD in verses 22–23?

events.title: God renews the promise
events.summary: The LORD tells Moses that Pharaoh will drive Israel out by a strong hand. God says he is the LORD, who made a covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He has heard Israel groan and remembers that covenant. He promises to free them, take them as his people, and give them the land. The people do not listen, because of crushed spirits and cruel slavery. Moses asks how Pharaoh will listen if Israel will not. The chapter lists the families of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, down to Aaron and Moses. The LORD again sends Moses to Pharaoh.
events.detail: Verses 6–8 hold seven promises that begin “I will.” They are the fullest promise in the book so far. Verse 9 reports that the people did not listen. The verse gives the cause, and it is not unbelief or rebellion. It is “anguish of spirit” and “cruel bondage.” The text does not blame them. God’s next word in verses 10–11 is to go on with the plan anyway.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The covenant promise includes belonging to God. The people cannot listen to Moses (verse 9). What two reasons does the verse give?

events.title: Staff and river
events.summary: The LORD makes Moses like God to Pharaoh, with Aaron as his prophet. He says Pharaoh will not listen, and Egypt will learn that he is the LORD. Moses is eighty and Aaron eighty-three. Aaron’s rod becomes a serpent before Pharaoh, and it swallows the magicians’ rods. Pharaoh’s heart stays hard. In the morning Aaron strikes the river, and its water turns to blood. The fish die, and the Egyptians dig for water to drink. The magicians do the same, and Pharaoh goes home unmoved.
events.detail: The first plague strikes the river, the source of Egypt’s water and fish. Pharaoh had used that river to kill Hebrew boys (1:22). Verse 20 says the blow came “in the sight of Pharaoh.” Verse 23 shows him walk back into his house. Verse 24 shows his people digging along the bank for water. The king refuses, and those under him carry the cost. Verse 5 states the aim of it all: Egypt will know who the LORD is.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Pharaoh goes into his house and does not take it to heart (verse 23). What must ordinary Egyptians do in verse 24?

events.title: Frogs, lice, and flies
events.summary: Frogs come up from the river and fill houses, beds, and ovens. Pharaoh asks Moses to pray and promises to let the people go. The frogs die, and Pharaoh hardens his heart. Aaron strikes the dust, and it becomes lice on people and animals. The magicians cannot copy it and say, “This is God’s finger.” Swarms of flies fill Egypt, but not Goshen, where Israel lives. Pharaoh offers a sacrifice inside Egypt, then a short trip into the wilderness. Moses prays, the flies leave, and Pharaoh again refuses.
events.detail: Pharaoh bargains twice in this chapter. In verse 25 he allows worship but only “in the land.” In verse 28 he allows the wilderness but not “very far away.” Each offer gives a little and keeps control. He also asks, “Pray for me,” while the flies are still there. Moses warns him in verse 29 not to deal falsely again. Verses 15 and 32 show the pattern: relief comes, and the promise ends.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Pharaoh says Israel may go, “only you shall not go very far away” (verse 28). What happens to his promise in verse 32?

events.title: Livestock, boils, and hail
events.summary: A disease kills Egypt’s livestock in the field, but none of Israel’s animals die. Moses throws furnace ashes into the air, and boils break out on people and animals. The magicians cannot stand before Moses. The LORD says he let Pharaoh stand to show his power in all the earth. He warns of heavy hail and tells Egypt to bring servants and animals inside. Some of Pharaoh’s servants fear the word and obey; others do not. Hail and fire strike all Egypt except Goshen. Pharaoh says he has sinned, but when the hail stops he hardens his heart.
events.detail: The hail is the first plague that comes with a way to escape. Verse 19 tells Egypt to bring people and animals under cover. Verses 20–21 then divide Pharaoh’s own servants into two groups. Some “feared the LORD’s word” and saved their workers and herds. Others left them in the field. So Egyptians are not treated as one mass, and some respond before their king does. In 10:7 those servants urge Pharaoh to give in.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Pharaoh says, “I have sinned this time” (verse 27). What does verse 34 say he did when the hail stopped?

events.title: Locusts and darkness
events.summary: The LORD says these signs are for Israel to tell their children and grandchildren. Moses warns of locusts, and Pharaoh’s servants beg him to let the men go. Pharaoh asks who will go, and Moses says everyone, with flocks and herds. Pharaoh will let only the men go and drives Moses out. Locusts eat every green thing the hail left. Pharaoh admits sin, the locusts are blown into the Red Sea, and he refuses again. Three days of thick darkness cover Egypt, but Israel has light. Pharaoh says to go but leave the animals, and Moses says not a hoof stays.
events.detail: Pharaoh has now offered four deals. Worship in Egypt, not too far, men only, and now people without animals. Each one keeps something of Israel’s in his hand. Flocks left behind would be a reason to return. Moses gives a different reason in verse 26: the animals are for the LORD. They do not yet know what he will ask for. So Moses will not agree to limits on worship before it begins.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Pharaoh will let the people go if the flocks stay (verse 24). Why does Moses say every animal must come in verse 26?

events.title: The final plague announced
events.summary: The LORD tells Moses that one more plague will make Pharaoh drive Israel out. The people are to ask their Egyptian neighbors for silver and gold. Moses is highly regarded in Egypt. He tells Pharaoh the LORD will go through Egypt about midnight. Every firstborn will die, from Pharaoh’s son to the slave girl’s at the mill. A great cry will rise, but not a dog will bark at Israel. Moses leaves Pharaoh in hot anger. The LORD hardens Pharaoh’s heart, and he still refuses.
events.detail: Verse 5 names the top and the bottom of Egypt. Pharaoh sits on a throne, and the servant woman sits behind a millstone. Both lose a firstborn, and so does the livestock. The servant had no part in Pharaoh’s decisions. In 4:22–23 God called Israel his firstborn and warned of this exact result. Pharaoh’s refusals in chapters 5–10 bring the loss on his whole land. The text reports the cry in verse 6 without softening it.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The plague reaches from the throne to the slave at the mill (verse 5). How do these deaths affect your reading of Israel’s freedom?

events.title: Passover and departure
events.summary: The LORD makes this month the first of the year. Each household must take a lamb without defect and kill it on the fourteenth day. They put its blood on the door posts and eat it roasted, dressed to leave. The LORD will strike Egypt’s firstborn and pass over the houses with blood. Israel must keep this day and seven days of bread without yeast, forever. At midnight every Egyptian house has someone dead, and Pharaoh tells Israel to go. They leave in haste with unrisen dough and Egyptian silver and gold. About 600,000 men leave on foot, with a mixed crowd, after 430 years.
events.detail: The rules for the meal are given before the rescue happens. Verses 14, 17, and 24 each say to keep it in later generations. Verse 26 expects a child’s question at the table. The answer in verse 27 says the LORD “spared our houses.” A parent born long after can still say “our.” So the meal lets each generation stand inside the night of leaving. Verse 11 keeps the hurry in it: belt on, sandals on, staff in hand.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the Passover lamb with Jesus Christ. Children will ask what the Passover service means (verse 26). What answer does verse 27 give?

events.title: Remembering and the pillars
events.summary: The LORD claims every firstborn male in Israel, human and animal. Moses tells the people to remember this day with seven days of unleavened bread. They must tell their sons what the LORD did when they left Egypt. Firstborn animals are sacrificed, and firstborn sons are bought back. God does not lead them by the near road through Philistine land. He says they might see war and return to Egypt. He leads them by the wilderness toward the Red Sea, and Moses carries Joseph’s bones. The LORD goes ahead in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night.
events.detail: Verse 17 says the short road was near and God did not use it. The reason is the people, not the distance. They might see war, change their minds, and go back to Egypt. So the route is fitted to what they can bear. Verse 18 notes they left “armed,” yet arms did not make them ready. Verses 21–22 add that they are not left to find the way alone. The cloud and fire never leave the front of the camp.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: God chose the longer road (verses 17–18). What reason does verse 17 give?

events.title: The sea crossing
events.summary: The LORD has Israel camp by the sea, so Pharaoh will think they are trapped. Pharaoh regrets freeing his slaves and chases them with six hundred chosen chariots. The people see the army, cry out, and tell Moses that serving Egypt was better. Moses says to stand still and see the LORD’s rescue. The cloud moves behind Israel, between the two camps. Moses stretches out his hand, and an east wind divides the sea all night. Israel crosses on dry ground with walls of water on each side. The Egyptians follow, the water returns, and not one of them is left.
events.detail: The people have only just left Egypt. In verse 12 they quote what they said there: “Leave us alone.” Slavery was hard, but it was known, and the sea and the army are not. So fear makes the old life look safe. Moses does not argue with them. He tells them to stand still and watch (verses 13–14). Verse 31 shows the change afterward: they fear the LORD and believe.
events.uncertainty: Lines join the places Exodus names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: First Nephi 17 recalls the sea crossing to teach trust in God. The people say serving Egypt was better (verse 12). What does Moses tell them to do in verses 13–14?

events.title: Songs and bitter water
events.summary: Moses and Israel sing to the LORD, who threw horse and rider into the sea. The song says the LORD is a warrior, and Pharaoh’s captains sank like a stone. It says the nations tremble and the LORD will plant his people on his mountain. Miriam the prophetess leads the women with tambourines and dancing. Israel then walks three days in the wilderness without water. At Marah the water is bitter, and the people grumble at Moses. The LORD shows Moses a tree that makes the water sweet. He promises health if they listen, and they camp at Elim’s twelve springs.
events.detail: Verses 1–21 are a long song of praise. Verse 22 follows with three days and no water. The singers of verse 1 are the grumblers of verse 24. The text does not hide how fast that happened. Their need is real, and the LORD answers it without rebuke in verse 25. He also calls this a test and adds a promise tied to listening (verse 26). Verse 27 ends with more water than they asked for: twelve springs.
events.uncertainty: Lines join the places Exodus names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Three days after the song, the people ask Moses what they will drink (verse 24). What does the LORD call himself in verse 26?

events.title: Manna and Sabbath
events.summary: In the second month Israel reaches the wilderness of Sin and complains of hunger. They say they wish they had died by the meat pots of Egypt. The LORD promises bread from the sky each day, as a test. Quail come at evening, and a fine flake covers the ground at dawn. Each person gathers an omer, and no one has too much or too little. What is kept overnight rots, except on the sixth day, when they gather double. On the seventh day there is none, because it is the Sabbath. They call it manna and eat it forty years.
events.detail: The bread comes with rules, and verse 4 calls them a test. Each household takes one omer per person (verse 16). Verse 18 gives the result: no one had extra, and no one lacked. Hoarding fails, since kept manna rots by morning (verse 20). So no one can store up an advantage over a neighbor. In Egypt they were measured by bricks made. Here they are measured by what each one needs to eat.
events.uncertainty: Lines join the places Exodus names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Church manual connects manna with reliance on God. Some gathered more and some less (verse 17). What does verse 18 say each one ended with?

events.title: Water and Amalek
events.summary: Israel camps at Rephidim, where there is no water. The people quarrel with Moses and say he brought them out to die. Moses cries to the LORD and says they are ready to stone him. He strikes the rock at Horeb before the elders, and water comes out. The place is named Massah and Meribah for their testing and quarrel. Amalek attacks, and Joshua leads the fight while Moses stands on the hill. Israel wins while Moses’ hands are up, so Aaron and Hur hold them until sunset. Moses builds an altar named “The LORD our Banner.”
events.detail: Verse 11 ties the battle to Moses’ raised hand. Verse 12 then admits a plain limit: his hands grew heavy. The fix is ordinary. Two men bring a stone for him to sit on and hold his arms. Joshua fights below, Moses holds the rod, and Aaron and Hur hold Moses. The account names every one of them. In verse 15 the altar’s name gives the credit to the LORD.
events.uncertainty: Lines join the places Exodus names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Moses cannot keep his hands up alone (verse 12). Who helps him, and how?

events.title: Jethro's counsel
events.summary: Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law and priest of Midian, hears what the LORD did for Israel. He brings Moses’ wife Zipporah and their two sons to the camp. Moses tells him everything, and Jethro blesses the LORD and offers sacrifices. The next day Moses judges the people alone from morning to evening. Jethro says this is not good and will wear out Moses and the people. He advises choosing honest, able men to judge small cases. Hard cases will still come to Moses. Moses does all this, and Jethro goes home.
events.detail: Jethro watches a full day of court before he speaks (verses 13–14). His worry in verse 18 is for two parties: Moses and the people. One judge means people stand waiting from morning to evening. Verse 21 sets the test for new judges: able, God-fearing, truthful, and hating unjust gain. Verse 23 names both gains. Moses will last, and the people “will go to their place in peace.” The advice comes from a Midianite priest, and Moses takes it (verse 24).
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Jethro tells Moses, “The thing that you do is not good” (verse 17). Who gains from his plan in verse 23?

events.title: At Sinai
events.summary: In the third month Israel camps before Mount Sinai. The LORD reminds them how he carried them on eagles’ wings. If they keep his covenant, they will be his own, a kingdom of priests. All the people answer that they will do what the LORD has spoken. They wash their clothes, and a boundary is set around the mountain. On the third day there is thunder, lightning, thick cloud, and a loud trumpet. The mountain smokes and shakes as the LORD comes down in fire. Moses goes up and is sent back to warn the people.
events.detail: God’s offer in verses 4–6 starts with what he has already done. He brought them out and “brought you to myself.” Only then comes the “if” of verse 5. So the covenant is offered to a freed people, not to slaves earning freedom. Verse 8 records their answer before any law is given. They agree to the relationship first and hear its terms in chapter 20. Verse 6 states their role toward others: a kingdom of priests.
events.uncertainty: Lines join the places Exodus names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The Church manual connects covenant belonging with duties of holiness and service. The people answer together in verse 8. What had God done for them before he asked (verse 4)?

events.title: The Ten Commandments
events.summary: God speaks and names himself as the one who brought Israel out of slavery. He commands no other gods, no idols, and no misuse of his name. The seventh day is a Sabbath of rest for children, servants, animals, and strangers. They must honor father and mother. They must not murder, commit adultery, steal, give false testimony, or covet. The people tremble at the thunder and smoke and stand far off. They ask Moses to speak for God, and Moses goes into the thick darkness. The LORD forbids gods of silver or gold and allows a plain altar of earth.
events.detail: Verse 2 comes before any command: God freed them from “the house of bondage.” The Sabbath command takes four verses (8–11). Verse 10 lists who may not be made to work: children, servants, animals, and strangers. The one addressed is the person with power to order others. So the day of rest limits what a master may demand. Egypt allowed no rest from bricks (5:5–9). Verse 11 roots the day in God’s own rest at creation.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual studies how each command can shape faithful choices. The Sabbath command names who must rest (verse 10). Who is on the list besides the head of the house?

events.title: Laws about servants and injury
events.summary: These are the rulings set before Israel. A Hebrew servant serves six years and goes free in the seventh. A daughter sold as a servant keeps rights to food and clothing, or goes free. Murder brings death, but an accidental killer may flee to a set place. Kidnapping and striking or cursing parents bring death. One who injures another pays for lost time and healing. A master who destroys a servant’s eye or tooth must free that servant. Owners pay for harm from an open pit or a bull known to gore.
events.detail: These rulings assume that some people are servants owned by others. Verse 21 calls the servant the master’s “property.” Within that world, verses 26–27 set a limit. A master who destroys an eye or knocks out a tooth loses the servant. The injured person goes free “for his eye’s sake.” So the servant’s body is protected, though the servant is not equal. Verse 2 adds a time limit: a Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: These laws come from an ancient legal setting. A servant who loses an eye goes free (verse 26). What does verse 21 show about the servant’s standing?

events.title: Property and vulnerable people
events.summary: A thief pays back more than he stole, up to five oxen for one. A person pays for crops ruined by his animal or his fire. Disputes over goods left in another’s care come before God. A man who seduces an unpledged virgin must pay a dowry for her. Israel must not wrong a foreigner, because they were foreigners in Egypt. God will hear the cry of any widow or fatherless child they wrong. Lenders must not charge the poor interest. A cloak taken as a pledge must be returned before sunset.
events.detail: A lender could hold a cloak as security for a loan. Verse 26 lets the pledge be taken but not kept overnight.
